basis: New mission, no workbook source; written per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, angle distinct from sdg4-1 (STEM/exam pressure) and sdg4-2 (digital equity/media literacy): the status and outcomes of vocational/technical education specifically. Facts and sources: vocational-school enrollment share fell from 59.6% (98th academic year) to 46.68% (112th academic year), a 16-year low; ratio was 7:3 forty-plus years ago; academic track overtook vocational in the 108th academic year; by the 113th academic year, general-track students ~279,000 (down 11,000) vs vocational students ~210,000 (down 52,000) (udn.com, CNA reporting Ministry of Education statistics, 2024-2025). Stigma ('black hands'/blue-collar label vs 'craftsman'/'technician' respect elsewhere) and parental credential-insistence even alongside direct-to-job tracks (Global Views Monthly, Liberty Times, CNA, 2024-2025). WorldSkills 2024 (47th, Lyon): Taiwan 58 competitors/50 trades, 2 gold/3 silver/10 bronze/28 excellence, 4th of 69 countries (Ministry of Labor press release Sep 2024, via udn.com/TBO Taiwan). WorldSkills Asia 2025 (Taipei, hosted by Taiwan): back-to-back overall team champion, 17 gold/9 silver/5 bronze/2 excellence youth + 5 gold junior, among 30 countries (Ministry of Labor 2025). Dual-Track Training Flagship Program (modeled on Germany's dual system): work 3+ days/week, school 2-3 days/week, 2021 cohort employment rate 94.9% (Workforce Development Agency). 2023 starting salaries: senior-high/vocational ~NT$28,000/month, university ~NT$33,000/month, graduate school ~NT$49,000/month; share starting at minimum wage: 58.3% senior-high/vocational, 23.9% university, 4.4% graduate school (Ministry of Labor 112-year new-hire wage statistics, via Global Views Monthly).

slides.1: Imagine confessing to your parents that you would genuinely prefer a vocational school over a university degree, when almost nobody voices that preference aloud. Why does admitting it still feel so shameful?
slides.2: SDG 4 commits every country to quality education for all, a promise that was never intended to describe a single approved path. Taiwan's technical and vocational education system trains genuine, employable skills, yet it rarely receives equal respect.
slides.3: Taiwan's manufacturing base depends on skilled technicians as much as on engineers. Yet enrollment in that very track keeps declining every year. By the 113th school year, technical programs held only about 210,000 students, well below past levels.
slides.4: The decline is striking. Forty years ago, roughly seven students in ten enrolled in a technical high school, yet general academic high schools have since overtaken vocational schools in total enrollment, a reversal nobody predicted.
slides.5: A harsh label still clings to these graduates, one that translates roughly as black hands, evoking a grease-stained manual laborer. In countries with genuinely strong vocational systems, that same worker earns the title of craftsman or technician instead.
slides.6: Even where a direct-to-employment technical program genuinely exists, many parents still insist their child also collect a university credential alongside it. A teenager who skips university risks being treated as a social outsider among peers.
slides.7: Now for some genuine pride. At the 2024 WorldSkills competition held in Lyon, France, Taiwan fielded 58 competitors across 50 trades, and the team collected 2 gold, 3 silver, and 10 bronze medals, finishing 4th among 69 competing countries.
slides.8: Taiwan subsequently hosted the 2025 WorldSkills Asia competition in Taipei. Its team has secured the overall championship for a second consecutive time, prevailing again among 30 competing countries and regions.
slides.9: A Dual-Track Training program is modeled on Germany's apprenticeship system. It requires students to work three days and attend class two or three days weekly. Its 2021 cohort reached a 94.9 percent employment rate that few university majors match.
slides.10: Instead of confining technical education to a classroom alone, more schools could adopt this dual model, blending paid work with structured study every week. Both sides gain something real from it.
slides.11: Outdated workshops with old machines hold learning back. Schools should invest in modern tools rather than only upgrading academic labs, so that skills taught match what factories actually use today.
slides.12: Middle school counselors could help reshape this culture as well. Instead of habitually presenting university as the default trajectory, they could frame a vocational path as an equally prestigious option from the very beginning of course selection.
slides.13: Here is where the real tension begins. If Taiwan's export factories depend this much on skilled workers, then a shrinking trade-school pipeline threatens the very industries that made the island famous, chip plants included.
slides.14: However, parental hesitation is not merely old-fashioned thinking here. In 2023, a new vocational hire earned around NT$28,000 monthly, while a university graduate earned roughly NT$33,000.
slides.15: However, that pay gap concentrates almost entirely at career entry. Roughly 58 percent of vocational new hires begin exactly at minimum wage, while only about 24 percent of university graduates start there.
slides.16: However, a starting salary rarely captures the full arc of a career. Skilled technicians, particularly those winning WorldSkills medals, frequently close or even reverse that early pay gap within a matter of years, not decades.
slides.17: So here is where matters genuinely stand today. Enrollment in technical schools keeps declining year after year, yet these same schools keep winning medals while placing graduates into steady jobs.
slides.18: This matters regardless of your own field of study. Taiwan's entire economy depends on both kinds of graduates functioning together, and neither pathway can genuinely thrive while the other is quietly starved of respect and resources.
slides.19: So start by questioning the hierarchy you were raised to accept without argument. Ask yourself honestly why a degree still feels safer than a skill, then share a WorldSkills story with someone who has genuinely never heard one.
slides.20: Two distinct paths built this island together, and both diplomas deserve equal respect, starting today, not eventually. Taiwan's future genuinely depends on every skilled hand it can find and keep.
